name: Network Service Discovery
dense_text: Technique: T1046 Network Service Discovery. Behavioral indicators: internal host or service enumeration after an adversary has gained access; port and service probes across hosts inside the victim environment; lateral network scanning used to identify reachable systems and services; Nmap or another scanner enumerating open ports from an internal source. Distinguishing conditions: The scan is internal, lateral, or explicitly post-compromise. name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
dense_text: Technique: T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol. Behavioral indicators: command-and-control traffic carried directly over ICMP; raw TCP or raw UDP socket communication with an external endpoint; custom binary protocol operating over TCP or UDP; transport-layer communication with no recognized application protocol; SOCKS or socket-based C2 communication outside normal application semantics; fixed-size or patterned lower-layer packets associated with remote control; network security signature identifying non-application-layer command and control; bidirectional C2 flow using an unusual lower-layer protocol. Distinguishing conditions: A lower-layer protocol directly carries C2 commands or data. The alert identifies ICMP, raw TCP, raw UDP, sockets, or a custom transport protocol without proving encapsulation. Protocol type or raw-socket behavior defines the C2 channel, regardless of port. The lower-layer protocol carries sustained C2 communication. Representative procedures: Operation Wocao used a custom protocol for command-and-control communication. name: Brute Force
dense_text: Technique: T1110 Brute Force. Brute force is clear, but the alert does not prove that many passwords were tried against one or a few accounts. Brute force is clear, but the alert does not prove reuse of one or a few passwords across many accounts. Representative procedures: Lazarus Group performed brute-force attempts against administrator accounts. Sandworm Team scripted RPC authentication attempts against multiple hosts. APT28 performed brute-force attacks to obtain account credentials. Turla used net use with a predefined password list to attempt connections to victim systems. Dragonfly attempted to brute-force credentials to gain access. OilRig used brute-force techniques to obtain credentials. FIN5 used GET2 Penetrator to identify remote login and hard-coded credentials. APT38 attempted account access through brute force when passwords or hashes were unavailable.
